newsitem.title: FRANCE: Papon banned from leaving France ahead of trial.
newsitem.headline: Papon banned from leaving France ahead of trial.

text.p: A court banned former cabinet minister Maurice Papon on Thursday from leaving France ahead of his trial for World War Two crimes against humanity which is due to begin in early October.
The court in the southwestern city of Bordeaux ordered Papon, 86, to hand over his passport and other identity documents and keep authorities informed of his movements outside Paris, where he lives.

Papon's attorney, Jean-Marc Varaut, announced he would appeal against the ruling though acknowledging it would be only a symbolic move because a decision on the appeal would come well after the start of the trial.
"This does not augur well for the trial. They are putting moral handcuffs on my client," Varaut told Reuters.
The travel ban had been requested by a state prosecutor and by Nazi-hunter Arno Klarsfeld, a lawyer representing relatives of Holocaust victims.

Papon is accused of ordering the deportation of 1,560 Jews, including 223 children, to Nazi death camps when he was secretary-general of the Bordeaux region in 1942-1944 under the pro-Nazi wartime Vichy regime.
After the war, Papon served as Paris police chief between 1958 and 1967 and was named budget minister in the 1970s before his wartime activities became known in 1981.

"This is a very positive decision and is not merely symbolic," said Michel Touzet, an attorney for civil plaintiffs in the case. "Now justice officials will be able to take action if Maurice Papon wants to leave the country."
But Marcel Rouxel, a second lawyer for Papon, said the travel ban request showed the state and civil plaintiffs wanted to make Papon the scapegoat for the entire Vichy regime.
"This decision is a minor detail, but I am nonetheless worried by the direction this trial is taking," Rouxel said.
"I fear that prosecutors and, apparently, the political powers want...to put Vichy in the dock, and that Papon is to be judged as the sole living incarnation of this era," he said.
The court made no mention of a request by civil plaintiffs to give Papon police protection from possible assassination attempts.

Wartime Paris police chief Rene Bousquet, who was charged with crimes against humanity for overseeing the arrest of thousands of Jews, was fatally shot by a publicity-seeking failed writer in 1993 before his trial could get underway.
